prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept. Create a Minecraft builder reference sheet, landscape 3:2, high resolution, plain light background, crisp vanilla Minecraft voxel blocks only, no characters or animals. Two views SIDE BY SIDE: LEFT straight-on front elevation, orthographic; RIGHT three-quarter view of the SAME COMPLETE eight-plot street at the SAME SCALE. Both views must show all eight plots, in the same left-to-right order, without cropping. Use the width of each panel for the long street; generous white space is fine. Skilled human builder quality: real massing, projecting porches, recessed framed openings, stepped block roofs with verges, eaves and ridges; sub-block stairs, slabs, fences, walls, trapdoors and lanterns. No smooth non-Minecraft architecture. Small plot numbers 0 through 7 beneath each view. Add a compact block-key footer naming principal materials by exact ids.
Site: sunny Mississippi cotton mill village about 1900. Exactly eight contiguous 12-block-wide plots, total 96 wide by 19 deep, 1–2 storeys except Queen Anne tower about 22 blocks high. Gravel-and-dirt lane across front. Different wood picket fences, each plot with centred gate, lantern posts every 12 blocks. Every house on brick or stone piers with raised porch.
Left to right:
0 dusty-blue clapboard double shotgun, white trim, oxblood tin front-gable roof. Two adjacent doors and tall shuttered windows, gingerbread brackets supporting shared porch, twin brick chimney at back.
1 pink-board Creole cottage, one steep dark cypress-shingle roof sweeping over full-width galerie on slim dark posts. Two pairs French doors with green board shutters. Brick chimney on west gable.
2 square two-storey ochre American Foursquare, dark hipped roof with front dormer, white belt course, full-width porch on brick-pedestal columns, brick side chimney.
3 finest superintendent Queen Anne: plum clapboard ground storey, cream fishscale-effect upper storey built from staggered birch slabs/stairs. Front cross gable beside three-stage square corner tower, glazed belvedere and tall copper pyramid cap. Wraparound porch with turned-post effect and spindle frieze, orange stained glass over door.
4 blue-grey gable-front-and-wing farmhouse, weathered cedar-brown roofs, porch in L angle.
5 dark vertical-board mule barn, red gambrel roof and cupola, hayloft door with hoist beam; block-built wagon under east lean-to, small fenced rear paddock.
6 gravel yard: open green-tin picnic pavilion on SIX log posts over long table, domed stepped brick bread oven with smoking stack, wooden water tank on braced legs and rain barrels underneath.
7 red-brick company duplex, stone sills and cornice, two adjacent front doors, two-storey porch on brick piers with upper gallery, low grey hipped roof, two rear brick chimneys.
Strict allowed palette by role (exact Minecraft ids; choose these to approximate historic materials):

Use white_wool only for blocky smoke if needed. Do not add other block materials. Historic tin/shingles/clapboard are represented using these vanilla materials, never custom textures.
changes: Generated with the built-in image tool and saved without post-processing as concept.png in the current directory.
The image is approximately 3:1 rather than 3:2. The front elevation is above the three-quarter view rather than beside it.

The palette retains every planned block, including blocks not visibly used. Added shape variants and cross-role materials are build interpretations; a raster image cannot establish exact Minecraft block identities or a complete hidden inventory.

The image uses stylized clapboard, fine window mullions, thin pickets, curved-looking wagon wheels and ornate porch details that do not consistently match vanilla block geometry. The wagon-wheel button entry is an approximation, not an identifiable rendered block.
All eight plot types appear in order, but the number labels are misplaced: the early plots are shifted and plot 3 is not correctly labeled.
The two views differ in spacing, proportions and details. Equal scale, a 96-by-19 footprint, 12-block plots, tower height and 12-block lantern intervals are not reliably represented.

The front lane is narrow, the plot boundaries are irregular, and several gates are absent or not centered. Some fence sections appear blue-green, which has no exact match among the supplied wooden fence blocks.
Several house foundations appear continuous or concealed rather than clearly separated brick or stone piers.
Plot 0 has two separated doors with a window between them rather than adjacent doors. Its two chimneys sit near opposite roof ends rather than forming a clear rear twin stack.
Plot 1 shows green-shuttered openings but does not clearly resolve two pairs of French doors. The roof reads as a main gable with a lower porch extension rather than one uninterrupted sweep.

Plot 3 has extensive cream cladding across the front and tower, with plum concentrated in the gable and recessed areas. The requested plum ground storey and cream fishscale upper storey are not clearly divided; the tower stages are simplified.
Plot 4 has a broad front porch and a simplified wing; the porch is not clearly confined to the inside angle of an L.
Plot 5's wagon is exposed beside the lean-to, its rear paddock is not clearly visible, and the hayloft hoist beam is small and ambiguous.
Plot 6's six pavilion posts cannot all be verified. The tank legs have little visible diagonal bracing, and the barrels beneath are partly obscured.
Plot 7 does not clearly show two adjacent front doors. Its grey roof resembles stone-brick stairs and slabs, so those planned foundation materials are also listed under roof.
Shrubs and flowers are much denser than the site description specifies. Individual flower species, small containers and concealed functional blocks cannot all be identified conclusively.
No beds, cauldrons, composter, smithing table, furnace or smoker can be positively identified; their inclusion in the role palette preserves the plan rather than claiming visible placement.
The footer adds material swatches and labels; some labels are malformed, and its yellow_terracotta swatch looks like orange wood rather than vanilla terracotta.
